outline.description: Sets the stage by explaining who the parties are, what AFL sought from both DOJ and OSC, the relevant statutes governing OSC’s authority and FOIA enforcement, and how the case reached the D.C. Circuit.
subtopics: Parties and objectives: AFL’s FOIA request to DOJ regarding emails tied to judicial recusal inquiries
Alleged DOJ policy: not searching employee emails without consent
Parallel proceedings: AFL’s FOIA suit against DOJ (records being produced; not at issue on appeal)
Request to OSC: demand for investigation under 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3) for arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholding
OSC’s initial denial: reliance on FOIA’s disciplinary-trigger provision, 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i), as preconditions not met
District court ruling: legal error in reading § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) as limiting § 1216; remand to OSC but ultimate dismissal for failure to state a claim
Appeal posture: AFL appeals dismissal; the D.C. Circuit orders supplemental standing briefing and reviews de novo
OSC authority under the Civil Service Reform Act: §§ 1214 (corrective actions), 1215 (disciplinary actions), 1216 (other misconduct including FOIA withholdings)
FOIA’s separate OSC referral provision: § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) (court-ordered production + fee award + specific questioning of arbitrariness triggers OSC disciplinary proceeding)

outline.chapter_title: Article III Standing and the Procedural-Injury Framework
outline.description: Explains the constitutional requirements for standing and how courts assess injury, causation, and redressability when a plaintiff alleges a statutory procedural violation.
subtopics: Constitutional baseline: injury in fact, causation, and redressability (Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife)
Procedural rights cannot stand alone: no standing for a procedural right in vacuo (Summers v. Earth Island Institute)

Relaxed standing in procedural-injury cases: courts may relax imminence and redressability, but not injury in fact or causation (Center for Law & Education v. Department of Education; Florida Audubon)
Pleading standard at motion to dismiss: plausible factual allegations for each standing element (Food & Water Watch v. Vilsack)
Application here: AFL frames OSC’s refusal as violating a procedural right and asserts two concrete informational injuries

outline.chapter_title: First Standing Theory: FOIA Records Deprivation Traceable to DOJ
outline.description: Analyzes AFL’s claim that OSC’s refusal to investigate caused AFL’s injury of not receiving DOJ records, focusing on traceability and redressability defects.
subtopics: AFL’s theory: OSC’s non-investigation under § 1216 prevented AFL from obtaining the FOIA records from DOJ
Traceability problem: any nondisclosure injury flows from DOJ’s actions, not OSC’s
Speculative causal chain: OSC might investigate → might pursue § 1214/§ 1215 action → MSPB might sanction → DOJ might change conduct
Independent actors not before the court: MSPB and DOJ choices break causation (FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine)
Enforcement discretion: courts generally cannot compel how OSC exercises prosecutorial discretion (Heckler v. Chaney)
Redressability gap: a favorable judgment against OSC would not very likely spur DOJ/MSPB actions necessary to deliver the records (Hecate Energy LLC v. FERC)
Binding-parties principle: redressability turns on orders binding parties, not persuasive effects on nonparties (Haaland v. Brackeen)
Conclusion: even under relaxed procedural-injury standards, causation and redressability are too attenuated

outline.chapter_title: Second Standing Theory: Informational Injury From OSC Investigation Notices
outline.description: Evaluates AFL’s claim that it was injured by not receiving information that would have accompanied an OSC investigation, and why the court found no statutory entitlement or likely remedy.
subtopics: AFL’s claim: entitlement to investigation-related information (notices and updates) analogous to § 1214 procedures
Informational-standing requirement: denial of information the statute entitles the plaintiff to receive (Akins; Public Citizen; ASPCA v. Feld)
No statutory entitlement under § 1216: even assuming § 1216(a)(3) mandates an investigation, it does not mandate disclosures to complainants
Discretionary nature of § 1214 procedures in § 1216 investigations: Carson v. U.S. Office of Special Counsel
No concrete injury: absence of a legal right to receive specific investigation information defeats informational standing
Redressability failure: ordering an investigation would not require OSC to provide § 1214-style notices in a § 1216 matter

outline.description: States the court’s final judgment and extracts practical lessons about standing when attempting to compel OSC enforcement related to FOIA issues.
subtopics: Judgment: vacatur of the district court’s merits ruling and remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
Unreached merits: the panel does not decide interplay between § 1216 and § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) or whether § 1216 mandates investigations
Key takeaway on standing: plaintiffs must connect a concrete statutory entitlement or a non-speculative causal path to redress by a judgment binding the defendant
Limits on leveraging third-party enforcement: speculative chains involving nonparty agencies and prosecutorial discretion will defeat causation and redressability
Informational standing caution: identify a clear statutory right to receive information; discretionary communications are insufficient
Strategic implications for litigants: vindicate FOIA disclosure through FOIA’s own remedies; do not rely on compelling OSC investigations to indirectly secure records
